bullets.text: Risk-on: leaning into risky assets, 45th night in a row, VIX normal at 15.8.
Your book holds 20 positions, heat moderate at 1.6%.
XHLD, BBOT, OCGN are flagged tonight and worth a look.

regime.title: Regime
regime.note: Is money flowing toward risk or away from it? Tonight's read on the market's mood.

about.heading: What decides it
about.body: Three inputs move the label: the VIX, its term structure, and high-yield credit spreads. The other seven inputs are tracked and shown but do not vote.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: “Risk-on” means money is flowing toward risk; the VIX is a fear gauge (lower is calmer). Open the drivers to see which inputs argued which way.

macro-drivers.title: Macro drivers
macro-drivers.note: The three inputs that actually decide the regime call, with their recent history.

about.heading: What they are
about.body: The 10y–2y Treasury spread (the recession watcher), the high-yield credit spread (are lenders scared?), and the VIX (the equity fear gauge).

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Each tile shows today's value, the one-day change, and the last 90 observations' trend.

inflation.title: Inflation
inflation.note: Is inflation near the Fed's 2% target, and does the bond market expect it to stay there?

about.heading: What they are
about.body: Core PCE (the Fed's preferred gauge) and headline CPI, each as the percent change over the same month a year earlier; and the 10- and 5-year breakevens, the inflation the Treasury market is pricing in.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: The 2% line is the target. A breakeven near it says expectations are anchored; the research skills use the 10-year breakeven as the ceiling on a thesis's terminal growth rate. Informational only: nothing here votes in the regime call.

regime-timeline.title: Regime timeline
regime-timeline.note: How the market's mood has shifted across recent nights.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Each dot is one nightly snapshot; higher means more fear (the VIX). Color is that night's verdict: green risk-on, red risk-off, amber mixed.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: A mood that just flipped is weaker evidence than one that has held for weeks; watch the streak rather than any single night.

candidates.title: Research candidates
candidates.note: A reading queue of good companies whose shares are currently marked down; nothing on it is a recommendation.

about.heading: What this screens for
about.body: Quality first: durable returns on capital, real free cash flow, a rising Piotroski score, and a share price currently well off its highs.

about.heading: How it differs from the scorecard
about.body: The scorecard below finds stocks doing something odd right now; this finds good businesses that happen to be cheap. Quality enters the funnel here; dislocation is only the timing.

about.heading: What happens next
about.body: Names go to deep research before any decision. List entries are graded for calibration only — see Candidates screen edge under Track record.

about.heading: The hidden columns
about.body: ROIC is the profit earned on the money invested in the business; FCF yield is the cash it throws off as a share of its price; F-score counts nine signs of improving health out of nine; RSI measures how oversold the shares are; accruals is how far reported earnings run ahead of cash, where negative is the good sign.

research-reopens.title: Research reopens
research-reopens.note: Researched names set aside, each with the evidence that would reopen the question.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: A dated trigger is usually an earnings report; “due” means that evidence now exists and the name deserves a fresh look. An event trigger waits on a filing or a price, with no date attached.

about.heading: Lifecycle
about.body: A row retires when the name is re-researched; the ticker links to the full thesis. Due rows lead the table, and the chip counts triggers dated within a week of today.

scorecard.title: Ticker scorecard
scorecard.note: Stocks doing something statistically odd right now, which says nothing about business quality.

about.heading: What this is
about.body: Every signal here is market microstructure — short interest, days-to-cover, oversold RSI, FTD spikes, retail chatter. A high score means something unusual is happening to the stock, usually a small one, and says nothing about the business.

about.heading: Why a crashing stock flags bullish
about.body: Deeply oversold RSI and crowded shorts vote bullish on a mean-reversion hunch. That hunch is worthless when the drop had a real cause: a stock down 40% on bad news will sit here flagged bullish every night until the price stabilizes.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: The bar is the summed vote, left of center bearish; Split is the raw bullish/bearish count; ★ marks strong agreement. Signals with data is the share of the signal set that had a reading for the name tonight. The chip counts the names that crossed the flag threshold and how many of those you already hold; it is a count, never a grade.

about.heading: How much to trust it
about.body: Treat it as a to-research feed: most flags deserve rejection, and by design the research step kills nearly everything. Whether any single signal has proven edge is graded under Signals; so far none has.

cot-tails.title: Crowded futures bets
cot-tails.note: Futures markets where the professional crowd is all-in on one side of its own 3-year range.

about.heading: What this is
about.body: Weekly CFTC managed-money positioning, each futures market measured against its own 3-year range. A row appears only when a market sits in the bottom or top 15% of that range with at least a year of report history behind it.

about.heading: Why per-market
about.body: The composite's class-average positioning signal cannot see one market's extreme inside a mixed class: the week sugar sat at the 12th percentile of its range, the softs class averaged 33 and scored nothing.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: A washed-out short is a coiled spring — any bullish surprise forces funds to buy back at once; a crowded long is the mirror. Neither is a direction call on its own: it marks where a squeeze has fuel, not when it fires.

rows.market: GASOLINE RBOB - NEW YORK MERCANTILE EXCHANGE

cot-tails.caveat: A tail marks a market to watch, not a trade: identical washouts have resolved violently or sat unchanged for months. No measured forward-return evidence yet.
cot-tails.empty: no futures market sits in the tail of its own 3-year managed-money range tonight

signal-recommendations.title: Signal recommendations
signal-recommendations.note: The verdict on each signal (keep, watch, or anti-signal), graded against the real base rate.

about.heading: Why the base rate matters
about.body: A randomly chosen scored ticker beat its benchmark only ~40% of the time over these windows, so a 61% hit-rate can still be worth nothing. Every verdict is measured against that baseline, not a coin flip.

about.heading: The verdicts
about.body: “Keep” means the whole confidence range sits above the baseline; “anti-signal” sits entirely below it (significantly wrong, never a win); “watch” straddles. The chip counts each signal once, at its longest graded horizon; the confidence-range bounds sit behind “more columns”.

about.heading: Hold it loosely
about.body: Several signals are graded at once, so a few clear the bar by luck. Re-weighting the catalog is always a human decision; nothing here feeds back automatically.

signal-recommendations.caveat: A backtest replay against ALFRED vintages, not live trading. Read excess and beats-baseline rather than hit-rate alone, and remember this is one history, not a distribution.
signal-recommendations.empty: insufficient evidence for every signal so far, which is expected of a young scorer; fills in once a signal's evidence crosses the reliability floor

signal-efficacy.title: Signal efficacy
signal-efficacy.note: Every signal's raw report card against simply holding SPY.

about.heading: What this is
about.body: How often each signal has been right so far, and by how much it beat the SPY benchmark. Unfiltered: every signal appears, proven or not.

about.heading: The chip and the verdict column
about.body: Keep means the signal beat chance with room to spare; watch means it is ahead but not yet clearly; anti-signal means it was reliably wrong; unproven means too few independent episodes to say. Each signal counts once, at its longest graded horizon.

about.heading: More columns
about.body: The folded columns hold the confidence interval around the hit rate, the chance-alone rate it is measured against, the number of distinct dates, and whether the signal was matched through a proxy class rather than the ticker.

signal-efficacy.caveat: Small sample; windows overlap, so one hot week can flatter several signals at once. Grades firm up as distinct composite dates accumulate.
signal-efficacy.empty: no matured signal outcomes yet; appears once a signal's flagged calls reach their grading horizon

bucket-performance.title: Bucket performance
bucket-performance.note: Did stronger conviction actually produce better forward returns?

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Every past opinion grouped by conviction bucket, strong-bull down to strong-bear, each graded against SPY. If conviction means anything, stronger buckets should do better; this checks that.

about.heading: The chip
about.body: Pools the strong buckets against the plain bull and bear buckets at the longest horizon, and compares how often each was right. It refuses to compare until each side holds five graded flags.

about.heading: Chance alone and better than chance
about.body: Chance alone is how often a random pick would have been right over that window; better than chance by is the bucket's hit rate minus that. Reliable marks buckets with enough independent episodes to trust the gap.

verdict.text: Too few graded flags to compare buckets

bucket-performance.caveat: Buckets group flags by strength, not by independence; the same overlapping-episode caveat applies within each bucket. Read the count before trusting a bucket's average.
bucket-performance.empty: no matured buckets yet; appears once conviction-bucketed opinions reach their grading horizon

equity-curve.title: Portfolio vs SPY
equity-curve.note: How $100 in your stock picks grew, next to $100 in SPY and $100 in cash.

about.heading: The three numbers
about.body: "Your picks" is how $100 put into your stock book would have grown. It is time-weighted: adding money never counts as a gain and taking money out never counts as a loss; only price moves count. "SPY" is what the same $100 did in the index over the same days. "Cash" is what it would have earned sitting in a savings account at the fed funds rate. The chip in the header is simple subtraction, your picks minus SPY, in percentage points.

about.heading: How to read the chart
about.body: All lines start at $100 on the first charted date. The book is every journaled stock position marked at each day's close, with cash left out. A buy joins at its fill price and a sale leaves at its fill price, so the line moves only when held positions move. Days with nothing held are dropped from both lines, and a holding that predates the journal (sold on record but never bought) is left out entirely.

about.heading: Why cash is a line
about.body: Daily fed funds (FRED's DFF) compounded over the same window, roughly what a T-bill fund or HYSA would have paid. SPY asks whether the picks beat the index; cash asks whether the money should be in the market at all.

verdict.text: Ahead of SPY by 2.4 points since Jul 6

human-filter.title: Human-filter tally
human-filter.note: When you chose which flags to act on and which to pass, did your judgment add anything?

about.heading: What a flag is
about.body: A night when the signals leaned hard enough on one stock to be worth a look. Every flag is graded later on what the stock did against SPY over 5, 10 and 21 trading days.

about.heading: Acted, passed, skipped
about.body: Acted means you traded in the flag's direction. Passed means you journaled a deliberate no. Skipped means the flag came and went with no journal entry, which is most of them.

about.heading: Gain had you followed it
about.body: What a trade in the flag's direction would have made against SPY, averaged per row. A row with fewer than 5 flags shows its count but no average, in the table and the tiles alike: three flags is not a trend. If the flags you skipped kept gaining and the ones you acted on did not, the filter is costing you; the chip states that comparison once both sides hold five flags.

verdict.text: Flags you skipped went on to gain +1.5% at 5 days

human-filter.caveat: Compares acted-on vs. passed-on flags from a still-small decision journal. A handful of trades can swing the comparison either way.
human-filter.empty: no matured flagged opinions yet; appears once an acted-on or passed-on flag reaches its grading horizon

regime-performance.title: Regime edge
regime-performance.note: Does the market-mood call itself predict forward returns?

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Each row is one mood at one horizon: did risk-on nights actually precede better returns than risk-off nights? The chip reads the risk-on row at the longest horizon, and waits for five graded nights before averaging.

regime-performance.caveat: Regime windows are contiguous stretches rather than independent draws; a single risk-on run dominates the sample until more regimes accumulate.
regime-performance.empty: no matured regime outcomes yet — appears once a market-mood window reaches its grading horizon

book-heat.title: Advisor book heat
book-heat.note: How much of your account is genuinely at risk right now.

about.heading: Money at risk on a bad day
about.body: Add up, across every open position, what a normal bad day would cost: each holding's usual daily swing (its ATR) times the shares held. That total, as a share of the book, is the headline. Elsewhere on this page the same number is called heat.

about.heading: What it is not
about.body: Not the stop-out loss: stops sit further out, so being stopped costs more. Positions counted says how much of the book the number actually accounts for; a holding missing its inputs is left out, and Feeds missing counts the data sources that did not report.

tiles.label: Money at risk on a bad day
Positions counted
tiles.band: positions with the inputs to price a bad day

tiles.label: Feeds missing
tiles.band: of the inputs the advisor needs

group-heat.title: Bets, not positions
group-heat.note: Correlated positions collapsed into single bets.

about.heading: Why
about.body: Two energy names are one energy bet: risk adds up within a group, and sizing that ignores this quietly doubles exposure. Hedges net out, so a protective put reduces what its bet has at risk.

about.heading: At risk
about.body: The dollars a normal bad day would cost the whole bet, and that as a share of the book: the same money-at-risk number the book card totals.

group-heat.empty: no group heat yet; appears once the advisor computes tonight's book

position-heat.title: Per-position heat
position-heat.note: Each holding's contribution to the risk totals above.

about.heading: At risk
about.body: Shares held times the stock's usual daily swing (ATR): the dollars a normal bad day would cost, not the loss if the stop triggers. The detail behind the book and bet totals. Signal lean is tonight's composite vote on the name; Volatility data old means the swing input is stale. Bet and price sit behind “more columns”.

disagreements.title: Disagreements
disagreements.note: Positions you hold that tonight's signals argue against.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Tickers where the score points the opposite way from an open position. “Strong” means the score is far enough from neutral to be worth a look. Treat it as a prompt to re-check the thesis rather than an exit order.

size-caps.title: Size caps
size-caps.note: A volatility-scaled ceiling on each candidate's size; the advisor only suggests, it never places orders.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: More volatile names get smaller ceilings, so a one-ATR bad day costs roughly the same dollars across positions. The warning marker means the cap exceeds current buying power.

your-trades.title: Your trades
your-trades.note: Every stock you bought or sold on purpose, and whether research backed it.

about.heading: What counts as a trade
about.body: One journaled stock fill: a buy, or a sell that closed one. Automatic fills (dividend reinvestment, recurring buys) are left out because nobody decided them. Options are graded on their own premium ledger, not here.

about.heading: Research-backed or freelance
about.body: Research-backed means the research skill said buy on that name before you filled, on the verdict date shown. Freelance means nothing recommended it: no research call and no matching signal.

about.heading: Result and the chip
about.body: Result is the return from your fill price to your exit price, so an open position shows a dash until you sell. The chip averages closed trades only, and refuses to grade until five have closed: one good exit is not a track record.

verdict.text: 2 closed trades, too few to grade

tiles.label: Backed by research
tiles.band: a buy verdict before the fill

your-trades.caveat: Grades the human's own fills from the journal. Coverage is whatever got journaled, and a result counts only once the position is closed.
your-trades.empty: no deliberate trades journaled yet; appears with the first journal-sync of a stock fill

trading-the-signals.title: Trading the signals
trading-the-signals.note: When you traded a flagged name, did you side with the signal, and what did the fill cost?

about.heading: Sided or against
about.body: Only trades on names the signals had an opinion about. Sided with the signal means you bought a bullish flag or sold a bearish one. Went against it means the opposite. No signal means the score was exactly neutral.

about.heading: Paid vs the plan
about.body: Your fill price against the closing price on the day the flag fired, which is the price the paper grade uses. Less means you paid under that close; more means the name had already moved by the time you filled. Days to fill is how long that took.

about.heading: Why several rows
about.body: Every trade is graded at three horizons (5, 10 and 21 trading days), and the table shows each. Averages stay blank until five trades have matured at that horizon.

tiles.label: Sided with the signal
tiles.band: 8 went against it · 0 had no signal

tiles.label: Paid vs the plan
tiles.band: vs the close when the flag fired

trading-the-signals.caveat: Only trades that answered a flagged opinion are graded here. Freelance and research-backed buys with no matching signal stay out.
trading-the-signals.empty: no flagged trade has reached a grading horizon yet

candidate-efficacy.title: Candidates screen edge
candidate-efficacy.note: Does the candidates screen's timing beat SPY after a name first enters the list?

about.heading: The two doors
about.body: Why it qualified is the growth test the name passed: 3y means three years of revenue growth, inflection means the last year and the forecast made up for a weak three-year record. What flagged it is the dislocation that timed the entry: an oversold RSI, a price drawdown, or both at once.

about.heading: How it is measured
about.body: A name's first entry onto the reading list starts a stopwatch: its 21- and 63-trading-day return is measured against SPY, split by which dislocation door let it in (oversold RSI, a price drawdown, or both at once).

about.heading: What it does not grade
about.body: Timing only, never the multi-year quality thesis behind the pick, and none of it feeds back into the screen's own gates.

tiles.label: Beat SPY
tiles.band: 21 trading days after joining the list

candidate-efficacy.caveat: Episodes are few and overlap early. The view carries plain averages with no confidence interval, so read n before believing any row.
candidate-efficacy.empty: no matured episodes yet; first grades appear ~21 trading days after the first screen night

health.title: Pipeline health
health.note: Did last night's machinery actually run, and is every database fresh?

about.heading: What it checks
about.body: Three layers: every scheduled job's last exit code and whether any is hung mid-run, FAILED/STALE markers in the last 24h of logs (as counts; the log itself stays on the host), and each database's newest snapshot age against its expected cadence.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Green with zero problems is the normal state. Any row here means a number elsewhere on this page may be stale, so check this section first when something looks off.

pending.title: In-flight opinions
pending.note: Opinions recorded but not yet old enough to grade.

about.heading: What this is
about.body: Every graded table above includes only matured outcomes. This is the queue still being measured; these rows become those grades once they age.

about.heading: Graded after
about.body: Each opinion is graded 5, 10 and 21 trading days after its entry date, so one flag sits here as three rows until the last of them matures. The grading date itself is only known once the closes exist.

verdict.text: 37,948 opinions from 46 nights waiting to be graded, the oldest from 2026-07-07

pending.caveat: These flags haven't reached their grading horizon yet, so nothing here is a result; it's a worklist.
pending.empty: nothing pending (everything registered so far has matured); fills once tonight's opinions are registered

basis-breaks.title: Data-integrity checks
basis-breaks.note: Price moves that look like data errors, caught before they can poison the grades; an empty table is the good outcome.

about.heading: What this is
about.body: Days where a price moved so far it looks like a stock split or a bad tick rather than a real move. Surfaced so a silent data problem cannot quietly skew every grade above. Move is the day's close over the prior close, so 0.50× is a halving; the newest 100 are listed and the chip carries the full count.

basis-breaks.empty: no basis breaks detected, which is the good outcome; fills only when a price move looks like a split or a bad tick

research-filter.title: Research call grade
research-filter.note: When the research skill said buy or pass, how often was it right against SPY?

about.heading: How it is measured
about.body: Every research-ticker verdict starts a stopwatch. A buy is right when the name beats SPY over the horizon; a pass is right when it lags. Hit rate is the share of calls that were right.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: This is the grade for the whole funnel's last step — the decision a human actually makes. Below 50% at n>30 means the research is adding noise, not signal.

research-filter.caveat: Hit rate is the safe headline; the excess column reads inversely on pass calls (a pass is right when the name lags), so compare it only within one call type.
research-filter.empty: no matured research verdicts yet; appears once a call's forward window closes

research-verdict-outcomes.title: Research calls, one by one
research-verdict-outcomes.note: Every graded research call with what the stock and SPY did afterward.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: One row per call and horizon. Excess is the stock's return minus SPY's; 'Right?' applies the call's own direction (a pass is right when excess is negative).

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: The grade above is an average; this is where you find the one call that dragged it, and whether the miss was a stock story or a market move.

research-calibration.title: Research call calibration
research-calibration.note: When the research said 70% it would beat SPY, did it beat SPY 70% of the time?

about.heading: The chip and the tiles
about.body: Every research call states how likely it is to beat SPY over a horizon. The chip compares the average confidence with the share of calls that actually won, once five have matured. Forecast error scores each call by how far its confidence sat from what happened: 0 is perfect, 0.25 is a coin flip, and lower is better. The tile also shows what always guessing the average win rate would have scored, which is the number to beat.

about.heading: The table
about.body: Calls are grouped by what they said, in ten-point bands. A well-calibrated forecaster's 60–70% band wins about 65% of the time. Distinct dates, behind the columns toggle, is how many separate days those calls were made: ten calls on one day are closer to one observation.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: Hit rate cannot tell a calibrated forecaster from a lucky one. Sizing up on conviction is defensible only once the stated confidence is shown to track reality; nothing here feeds back into gates or sizing.

research-calibration.caveat: Forecast error below the base-rate score means the stated confidence carries information; above it, always guessing the average would have done better. Bins stay tiny for months, so read Calls before the rates.
research-calibration.empty: no matured verdicts carry a stated probability yet

flag-response.title: What you did with each flag
flag-response.note: Each composite flag, whether you acted or passed, and how the name moved afterward.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: 'acted' means a fill landed on the flagged name, 'passed' means you logged a deliberate no, 'inferred' means no record either way. Directional excess is the return in the flag's direction, minus SPY.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: This is the row-level detail behind the 'Filter edge' tally: if the passes outperform the acted rows, your filter is subtracting value.

flag-response.empty: no matured flags yet; appears once a flagged name reaches its grading horizon

signal-effective-n.title: How much evidence, really
signal-effective-n.note: The signal report cards count rows; this counts independent episodes, which is the honest sample size.

about.heading: The problem
about.body: A signal that fires on ten consecutive days produces ten overlapping forward windows. They mostly share the same market weeks, so ten rows is closer to one observation.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: 'Distinct dates' collapses same-day rows; 'independent episodes' also merges runs of consecutive dates whose windows overlap. The sparkline is the hit rate on each flag date — a grade earned on one hot week shows as a single spike.

verdict.text: 12 of 23 signals rest on fewer than 3 independent episodes

signal-effective-n.caveat: A signal that fired on ten overlapping days is one observation, not ten. Trust the episode count over the row count.

candidate-outcomes.title: Candidates list, entry by entry
candidate-outcomes.note: What each name did against SPY after it first appeared on the candidates list.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: One row per list entry and horizon. 'Door' is which dislocation test let the name onto the list — an oversold RSI, a drawdown from the high, or both.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: The screen's edge is an average over these rows. A single large winner can carry it, so scan the distribution before trusting the summary.

candidate-outcomes.empty: no matured list entries yet; appears 21 trading days after a name first enters the candidates list

candidate-quality-trend.title: Falling-knife check
candidate-quality-trend.note: For every name still on the candidates list, whether the business has weakened since it first appeared.

about.heading: What a falling knife is
about.body: A stock that looks cheaper every week because its price is falling faster than its earnings — the cash-flow yield rises while the F-score or return on capital drops. The level gates keep passing it; only the trend shows the problem.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: 'What weakened' names the gates that fell since the first sighting; the before-and-after numbers sit behind 'more columns'. Flagged rows sort to the top; they are the names to re-research before buying more.

about.heading: The gates
about.body: F-score is a nine-point financial-health checklist; ROIC is the profit earned on the capital invested; FCF yield is spare cash as a share of the price; accruals are earnings that have not yet shown up as cash.

candidate-quality-trend.empty: no candidate has been on the list for two sightings yet

option-pnl.title: Option premium P&L
option-pnl.note: Dollar profit on single-leg option trades, kept separate from the stock grades.

about.heading: How it is measured
about.body: Every option fill is a signed cash event in the premium ledger; a position's P&L is those events summed once it closes or expires. Premium return is P&L over the premium at risk.

about.heading: Why it is separate
about.body: Options are graded on dollars, stocks on return versus SPY — the two never mix, so a lucky expiry cannot flatter the stock-picking grade.

option-pnl.empty: no option fills journaled yet; appears with the first single-leg option fill synced into the journal

replay-efficacy.title: Backtest replay
replay-efficacy.note: Would the macro signals have worked in the past, using only the data that existed at the time?

about.heading: How it is measured
about.body: Each FRED series is replayed from its ALFRED vintages — the numbers as first published, before revisions — and each flag is graded on what SPY (or a sector ETF) did next. A report enters the replay only after its release date.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Drift alone is how often the benchmark simply rose over that horizon; better than drift by is the flag's hit rate minus that. 'Beats drift' means the whole confidence interval sits above the drift; 'anti-signal' means it sits entirely below — a signal reliably wrong is not a signal to flip.

about.heading: The hidden columns
about.body: Behind the columns toggle: how many days the flag was on, the confidence interval around the hit rate, the drift figure itself, and the chance of a fluke — how often shuffled data produced a hit rate this good, so 0.04 means about one time in twenty-five.

replay-efficacy.caveat: Nominal and uncorrected across ~48 comparisons; a lone 'beats drift' at p≈0.04 is what chance produces. Read excess against the baseline, never hit rate alone — the benchmarks drift up, so a bullish flag 'wins' by doing nothing.
replay-efficacy.empty: no replay yet; runs Saturdays after the ALFRED vintage pull

replay-baseline.title: Benchmark drift
replay-baseline.note: How often each benchmark simply went up over each horizon — the bar every replayed flag has to clear.

about.heading: Why it exists
about.body: Stocks drift upward, so a bullish flag that does nothing still 'wins' most windows. Every replay grade is measured against this drift, never against 50%.

about.heading: The columns
about.body: Days measured is how many start dates were tested. Went up and went down are the share of those windows where the benchmark finished higher or lower; they need not sum to 100% because some windows end flat.

replay-flags.title: Replay flags today
replay-flags.note: What each replayed signal is saying right now, with its score over the last 90 flag days.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Score is the flag's vote: positive bullish, negative bearish, zero quiet. The sparkline shows how long it has held that view.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: This is the live edge of the backtest — the same signal definitions the replay graded, applied to the newest vintage.

exit-advice.title: Exit suggestions
exit-advice.note: For each holding, where a stop would sit and whether the size has outgrown the signals behind it.

about.heading: How it is computed
about.body: The stop is the price after a one-ATR adverse day from here; 'room to stop' is how far away that is. A trim appears when the position is larger than the advisor's cap for its current score.

about.heading: What to do with it
about.body: Nothing automatic happens. Read a trim as 'the signals no longer support this size' and a tight stop as 'one bad day is close' — then decide.

exit-advice.caveat: Decision support only. A stop here is a suggested distance from a one-ATR adverse day, not an order anywhere.
exit-advice.empty: no positions in the latest snapshot

option-heat.title: Option legs
option-heat.note: Each option position's share-equivalent exposure and what a one-ATR move would cost.

about.heading: How it is computed
about.body: Delta is how much the option moves for a $1 move in the stock, so delta × contracts × 100 is how many shares the leg acts like; 'at risk' is that many shares moving one ATR. A protective put counts negative and offsets the shares it covers in the group view.

about.heading: Uncovered legs
about.body: A leg with no delta input or a short leg is marked uncovered — its risk is unknown or open-ended, so the book heat number above it is a floor, not a total.

option-heat.empty: no option legs held in the latest snapshot

order-queue.title: Order queue
order-queue.note: Buys you have queued that have not yet been placed.

about.heading: How it works
about.body: You queue a buy with a reference price and a maximum gap; the morning slot places it at the open only if the live quote is within that band, otherwise it vetoes and the row lands in the run results.

about.heading: Why it is on the page
about.body: A queued order is a pending commitment of real money — it should never be a surprise the next morning.

order-queue.empty: the queue is empty; nothing will be placed at the next open

order-runs.title: Execution runs
order-runs.note: Every queued order the executor has processed and what happened to it.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: 'placed' means an order went to the broker under the limit ceiling; a veto names the gate that stopped it (price gap, cap, market closed). Outcome is the broker's final state where known.

order-reconciliation.title: Unreconciled orders
order-reconciliation.note: Orders the executor placed that the journal has not yet seen a fill for.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: The journal is what the grades run on. A placed order with no fill row means either the broker never filled it or the nightly journal sync missed it — both need a look.

verdict.text: every placed order has a journal fill

order-reconciliation.empty: every placed order has been matched to a journal fill

week-ahead.title: This week
week-ahead.note: Every scheduled release and earnings report this week, plus the Fed and expiry dates that shape it.

about.heading: What is in it
about.body: Economic releases from the official calendar, confirmed earnings dates, the next FOMC meeting and whether the Fed is in its pre-meeting quiet period, the next monthly options expiry, and the next early market close.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: A high-impact release or an FOMC day is the most common reason a signal moves for reasons that have nothing to do with the stock.

yield-curve.title: Treasury yield curve
yield-curve.note: Short and long Treasury yields and whether the curve is inverted, straight from the Treasury's daily table.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Normally the 10-year pays more than the 2-year. When it pays less the curve is 'inverted' — historically a recession warning, though the timing is loose.

federal-debt.title: Federal debt and the Treasury's cash
federal-debt.note: Total public debt and the government's checking-account balance over the last 90 days.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: When the Treasury rebuilds its cash balance it drains reserves from the banking system; when it spends it down it adds them. Either way it is liquidity moving in the background of every price.

funding-markets.title: Funding markets
funding-markets.note: Overnight rates and the Fed's balance sheet — the plumbing that shows stress before prices do.

about.heading: Overnight lending rate
about.body: SOFR is the rate banks actually paid to borrow cash overnight against Treasuries.

about.heading: Rate the Fed pays banks
about.body: IORB is what the Fed pays banks on the reserves they leave with it, the floor the overnight rate should sit near.

about.heading: Gap between them
about.body: Overnight rate minus the Fed's rate: above 0.05 points means banks are paying up for cash, which is the first sign of funding stress.

about.heading: Overnight lending volume
about.body: Billions of dollars borrowed overnight that day, the size of the market the rate is set in.

about.heading: Fed's holdings
about.body: The Fed's own bond portfolio in trillions; falling means the Fed is draining money from the system.

about.heading: Reverse repo
about.body: Cash that money funds parked at the Fed overnight because nothing else paid more, in billions.

tiles.label: Reverse repo parked at the Fed

fred-series.title: FRED series
fred-series.note: Every tracked economic series with its year-over-year change and how unusual today's level is.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Z-score is how many standard deviations the latest value sits from the series' own history — beyond ±2 is rare. The tiles are the regime's raw inputs; the regime card above turns them into a verdict.

verdict.text: 8 series unusually far from their own history

about.heading: The three reports

about.heading: More columns

short-volume-ratio.title: Heaviest short selling today
short-volume-ratio.note: Symbols where an unusually large share of today's volume was short sales.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: FINRA reports each day's short volume per symbol. A high ratio can mean bearish conviction — or market makers hedging heavy call buying. The sparkline shows whether it is new.

short-volume-ratio.empty: no symbol above the short-ratio threshold today

short-volume-streaks.title: Sustained short pressure
short-volume-streaks.note: Symbols that have stayed above the short-ratio threshold for the most consecutive days.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: One heavy day is noise; a streak is a campaign. These are the names where the short side has been leaning for weeks.

short-interest-crowded.title: Most crowded shorts
short-interest-crowded.note: Symbols where it would take the longest to buy back every short share at normal volume.

about.heading: What days-to-cover means
about.body: Shares short divided by average daily volume. Ten days means shorts need two weeks of the entire market's volume to exit — the fuel for a squeeze.

unusual-options.title: Unusual option activity
unusual-options.note: Option contracts that traded far more today than exist in open interest.

about.heading: Today's volume vs contracts held
about.body: How many times today's trading exceeded the contracts held (open interest). Above 1× means more changed hands than existed, so it is new positioning, not old positions closing. Whether it is a bet or a hedge is not visible.

about.heading: Implied volatility
about.body: Implied volatility is the size of the move the option's price is betting on, as a yearly percentage: 84% means the market is pricing swings of roughly that much over a year.

options-sentiment.title: Options-market mood
options-sentiment.note: The fear gauge, the put/call ratios and the VIX term structure — the regime's raw Cboe inputs.

about.heading: What the numbers are
about.body: The VIX is the market's expected 30-day swing; above 25 is fear, below 20 calm. Put/call above 1 means more hedging than betting. VIX above VIX3M ('backwardation') means the next month scares people more than the quarter.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: These three are the regime card's voters, shown here raw so you can see how close the call was.

dealer-positioning.note: What the Fed's primary dealers hold, from the NY Fed's weekly survey.

earnings-confirmed.title: Confirmed earnings dates
earnings-confirmed.note: Upcoming earnings reports whose dates the company has confirmed, not estimated.

about.heading: Why confirmed matters
about.body: Estimated dates slip. A confirmed date is when the options market's implied move becomes a real deadline for any thesis on the name.

earnings-confirmed.empty: no confirmed earnings dates in the window

market-closures.title: Market holidays
market-closures.note: Upcoming NYSE and bond-market closures and early closes, the days the order executor must not expect a normal open.

about.heading: Why it is under Ops
about.body: The order executor and every trading-day calculation key off the NYSE rows. An early close ends the intraday window early. Bond rows are context for Treasury auction timing — NYSE stays open on bond-only holidays like Columbus and Veterans Day.

energy-inventories.title: Energy inventories
energy-inventories.note: Weekly US crude, product and gas stocks with the change from last week and a year's trend.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: A draw (negative change) tightens supply and supports prices; a build does the opposite. The sparkline shows the seasonal pattern the weekly number sits inside.

about.body: The share of a year's consumption sitting in storage at year end: 43% means about five months of use is on hand. Low means a thin cushion, so prices react hard to a bad harvest.

glossary.Screener: one of the small programs here that visits a single official data source and files away what it finds. There are about seventeen, one per source.
glossary.Monitor: like a screener, but instead of measuring today it keeps a calendar of upcoming events: central-bank meetings, company earnings dates, market holidays.
glossary.Combiner: a program that reads what the screeners and monitors collected and derives something from it: an overall market opinion, a stock scorecard, a report card on past opinions. Combiners never fetch anything from the internet.
glossary.Market regime: a one-line summary of the market's overall mood (roughly: calm, nervous, or stressed), distilled from many indicators at once.
glossary.Z-score: a way of saying "how unusual is today's number compared with its own history?" Zero means perfectly typical; +2 or −2 means rare. Used here to spot readings worth a second look.
glossary.Short interest: how many of a company's shares investors have borrowed and sold, betting the price will fall. High short interest means many people are betting against the stock.
glossary.Fails-to-deliver: trades where the seller didn't hand over the shares on time. Occasional fails are plumbing noise; persistent ones can hint at stress or heavy short-selling in a stock.
glossary.FTD: trades where the seller didn't hand over the shares on time. Occasional fails are plumbing noise; persistent ones can hint at stress or heavy short-selling in a stock.
glossary.Dark pool: a private marketplace where large investors trade shares away from the public exchanges. The trades are real and eventually reported; "dark" refers to the order book not being publicly visible.
glossary.ATS: a private marketplace where large investors trade shares away from the public exchanges. The trades are real and eventually reported; "dark" refers to the order book not being publicly visible.
glossary.Put/call ratio: compares the volume of bets that prices will fall (puts) against bets that they'll rise (calls). An unusually high ratio suggests widespread nervousness.
glossary.VIX: a widely quoted index of how much turbulence traders expect over the next month, often called the market's "fear gauge." Low ≈ complacent; high ≈ frightened.
glossary.OPEX: options-expiration day, when a large batch of options contracts expires at once (typically the third Friday of the month). Markets can behave oddly around it, so the calendar here tracks it.
glossary.Yield curve: the pattern of interest rates on government debt from short loans to long ones. Normally longer loans pay more; when the curve "inverts" (short rates above long rates), it has historically preceded recessions.
glossary.COT / positioning: the Commitments of Traders report, a weekly government publication showing what large professional traders are betting in futures markets. Extreme positioning can mark crowded trades.
glossary.Backtest: replaying the system's rules against past data to see how they *would* have done — using only the information that was actually available on each historical day, so the replay can't cheat by peeking at the future.
glossary.Forward return: how a stock actually performed in the weeks *after* the system flagged it. "Paper" means graded on the record only; no money moved.
glossary.paper outcome: how a stock actually performed in the weeks *after* the system flagged it. "Paper" means graded on the record only; no money moved.
glossary.Settings UI: `uv run python config_ui.py`; a local browser page that edits `.env` (the file holding your keys and tuning knobs) safely, with API keys shown masked.
glossary.ATR: a measure of how much a stock typically bounces around in a single day. Higher ATR means more volatility; used here to size positions—bigger ATR, smaller bet.
glossary.average true range: a measure of how much a stock typically bounces around in a single day. Higher ATR means more volatility; used here to size positions—bigger ATR, smaller bet.
glossary.Book heat / Heat: a summary of how much money is riding on your current holdings, adjusted for market swings. High heat means concentrated risk; useful for knowing whether the portfolio is humming quietly or wearing thin.
glossary.Coverage: how much of the full picture actually has data behind it. On the ticker scorecard it's the share of the signals that could have had an opinion on a stock tonight that actually did — low coverage means the score rests on just a few inputs, not the whole roster. On the book-heat panel it's the share of your holdings' value where a real risk read (an ATR) was available to size it — low coverage means the heat number is missing pieces of the book.
glossary.Hit rate: in the backtester's report, the percentage of time the system's opinion was right (price went the way it was flagged). Always read alongside the benchmarks—if prices drift up anyway, a bearish flag "wins" by doing nothing.
glossary.Confidence interval: a range around a measured result that's probably correct, expressed as "the true answer is here about 95% of the time." A wide interval means less certainty; a narrow one means more.
glossary.CI: a range around a measured result that's probably correct, expressed as "the true answer is here about 95% of the time." A wide interval means less certainty; a narrow one means more.
glossary.Piotroski score: a simple nine-factor check of a company's financial health, ranging from 0 (weak) to 9 (strong). Looks at profitability, asset quality, and cash flow—rough, but a useful beginning-of-funnel filter.
glossary.Risk-on / risk-off: the market's mood in broad strokes. "Risk-on" means investors are buying stocks and taking chances; "risk-off" means they're retreating to safe havens like bonds and cash.
glossary.Score: the nightly sum of a ticker's signal votes. Positive means more bullish signals fired than bearish ones. The size says how lopsided the vote was, not how far the price will move.
glossary.composite score: the nightly sum of a ticker's signal votes. Positive means more bullish signals fired than bearish ones. The size says how lopsided the vote was, not how far the price will move.
glossary.Base rate: how often the benchmark moved that way anyway. A hit rate only means something when it beats this number; otherwise the "wins" were just the market drifting.
glossary.Edge: hit rate minus base rate. A positive edge means the signal called direction better than the market's own drift; zero means it added nothing.
glossary.Excess: how much better or worse a stock did than the benchmark over the same stretch. Positive excess means it beat the market, not just that it went up.
glossary.excess return: how much better or worse a stock did than the benchmark over the same stretch. Positive excess means it beat the market, not just that it went up.
glossary.Directional excess: excess return counted in the direction the signal called. A bearish flag earns positive directional excess when the stock does *worse* than the market.
glossary.RSI: a 0-to-100 gauge of how hard a stock has been bought or sold lately. Below about 30 usually reads as oversold; above 70, overbought.
glossary.relative strength index: a 0-to-100 gauge of how hard a stock has been bought or sold lately. Below about 30 usually reads as oversold; above 70, overbought.
glossary.ROIC: how much profit a company earns on each dollar tied up in the business. A steady double-digit ROIC is a mark of quality.
glossary.return on invested capital: how much profit a company earns on each dollar tied up in the business. A steady double-digit ROIC is a mark of quality.
glossary.FCF yield: the spare cash a business generates in a year, divided by the stock-market value of its shares (market cap). Higher means each dollar of cash costs you less to own.
glossary.free cash flow yield: the spare cash a business generates in a year, divided by the stock-market value of its shares (market cap). Higher means each dollar of cash costs you less to own.
glossary.Market cap: the total price tag on all of a company's shares put together.
glossary.market capitalization: the total price tag on all of a company's shares put together.
glossary.Reverse DCF: instead of guessing what a stock is worth, hold the cash-flow assumptions fixed and solve for the yearly return today's price already bakes in. A high implied return on cautious assumptions is interesting; a low one on rosy assumptions is a warning.
glossary.implied return: instead of guessing what a stock is worth, hold the cash-flow assumptions fixed and solve for the yearly return today's price already bakes in. A high implied return on cautious assumptions is interesting; a low one on rosy assumptions is a warning.
glossary.Hurdle: the return an investment has to beat to be worth the risk: the safe Treasury rate plus a premium scaled by beta — the stock's exposure to market-wide swings, not its own choppiness. An implied return only means something next to this number.
glossary.cost of equity: the return an investment has to beat to be worth the risk: the safe Treasury rate plus a premium scaled by beta — the stock's exposure to market-wide swings, not its own choppiness. An implied return only means something next to this number.
glossary.Equity risk premium: the extra yearly return investors demand for holding stocks instead of Treasuries. Damodaran re-solves it monthly from the market's own level; it is the market-wide half of the hurdle.
glossary.ERP: the extra yearly return investors demand for holding stocks instead of Treasuries. Damodaran re-solves it monthly from the market's own level; it is the market-wide half of the hurdle.
glossary.Terminal value: the part of a valuation covering everything past the forecast years, usually most of the total. It leans on a "forever" growth rate, which is why that one assumption gets policed hardest.
glossary.Terminal growth: the forever growth rate inside the terminal value. Capped at the Treasury rate (nothing outgrows the economy forever), and real growth above inflation has to be paid for with reinvested earnings.
glossary.Enterprise value: the market value of a company's equity and debt together, net of its cash: what buying the whole business would cost, not just its shares.
glossary.EV: the market value of a company's equity and debt together, net of its cash: what buying the whole business would cost, not just its shares.
glossary.Beta: a stock's exposure to risk that diversification can't remove: how much it moves with the market, standardized around 1. Not the same as volatility — a wild mover that ignores the market can still have a low beta.
glossary.Reinvestment rate: the share of profit plowed back into the business instead of flowing out as free cash. Growth has to be paid from here: growth rate = reinvestment rate × return on that reinvested capital.
glossary.Data age: how many days old the freshest input behind a number is. Small means current; large means the reading is running on stale data.
